pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 5–7 — know a coast/beach is where land meets the ocean, and that coasts can be sandy, rocky, or muddy, each with different plants and animals.
• Standards — UK (DfE KS1): Y2 'identify that most living things live in habitats to which they are suited' and 'identify and name a variety of plants and animals in their habitats, including micro-habitats' — different coast types are different habitats; also links to KS1 geography (physical feature: coast, beach, sea).
• Standards — US (NGSS): K-ESS3-1 / 2-LS4-1 — organisms live where their needs are met; compare life across different habitats (sandy vs rocky vs muddy shore).
• Operational details: this is a NAMING + HABITAT-MATCHING topic. Core moves: define 'coast' as the meeting line of land and sea; recognise three shore types by their material; and match a plausible animal to each (crab/limpet on rocks, sanderlings/razor shells on sand, wading birds/worms/mudskippers on mud). Keep it observational and photographic; save tides/erosion mechanisms for the 7–9 dependent.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (~5–6): points to where land meets sea and names 'beach/coast'; Tier B (~6–7): names ≥2 coast types and one animal at each; Tier C (~7): explains simply why a certain animal suits a certain shore (crab hides in rock cracks; wader probes soft mud for worms).
bestPractices: Anchor 'coast' as the LINE where land meets ocean using real aerial/photo imagery before naming shore types — place first, categories second.
Compare the three shore types side by side with real photographs so 'sandy / rocky / muddy' are distinguished by what they're made of, not by colour alone.
Pair each shore with a signature, verifiable resident (rocky = crab/limpet/anemone; sandy = sanderling/razor shell; muddy = wading bird/lugworm) so habitat and inhabitant are learned together.
Draw on children's own beach experiences ('what did you find at the beach?') to ground new vocabulary in memory.
Introduce the suited-to-habitat idea lightly ('why do crabs like the rocks?') as a bridge to Y2 habitats without heavy mechanism.
keyRepresentations: Three side-by-side shore photographs (sandy / rocky / muddy), each labelled
A 'where land meets the ocean' cross-section from dunes/cliffs down to the water
Habitat-and-resident cards pairing each shore type with a signature animal
A map/aerial view showing the coastline as a line around the land
commonMisconceptions: 'A beach is always sandy' — not knowing rocky and muddy shores are also coasts.
'The coast is just where you swim' — missing that the coast is the meeting line of land and sea, including cliffs and mudflats.
'The same animals live on every shore' — not connecting a shore's material to which animals suit it.
Confusing coast with the open ocean, or with a river bank/lake edge.
Thinking muddy shores are 'dirty/empty' when mudflats are rich in worms and feeding birds.

learn.summary: For ages 5–7: a coast is where land meets the ocean, and coasts can be sandy, rocky, or muddy — each a different habitat with different plants and animals. This is a naming and habitat-matching topic: define 'coast' as the land–sea boundary, recognise the three shore types by what they are made of, and match a typical plant and animal to each (seaweed with crab/limpet/anemone on rock; marram grass on the dunes behind the beach with sanderling/razor shell/cockle on sand; saltmarsh plants such as samphire with curlew/lugworm on mud). These are typical examples, not strict rules: some animals, such as crabs, lugworms and wading birds, can live on more than one kind of shore. Keep it observational and photographic; tides and erosion mechanisms are saved for older learners. The core insight is that one coastline can hold three very different neighbourhoods, and each plant or animal lives where it can meet its needs.

activities.title: Pan the changing coastline and reveal who lives there
feedback: If the learner says every coast is sandy, pan back to the rocky and muddy stretches: 'This is a coast too — and it is not sand. What is it made of?'
When they match an animal to a shore, confirm with the reason: 'Yes — the crab fits here because the rocks give it cracks to hide in.'
If they call mud 'dirty' or 'empty', reveal the worms and feeding bird: 'The mud is soft and full of hidden food — that is why the bird comes here to dig.'
If they point only to where people swim, trace the whole coastline: 'The coast carries on here, and here — all the way the land touches the sea.'
activities.rationale: A single labelled panorama that transitions across the three shore types lets young learners anchor the place first (land meets sea) and the categories second, with habitat and inhabitant learned together. Optional flaps and tap-to-reveal creatures make the 'suited to habitat' idea concrete without heavy mechanism, keeping cognitive load appropriate for 5–7.
sourceClaims: UK KS1 Y2 science requires pupils to identify that most living things live in habitats to which they are suited, and to identify and name a variety of plants and animals in their habitats including micro-habitats.

Rocky, sandy and muddy shores are distinct intertidal habitats supporting different communities of plants and animals (e.g. limpets and crabs on rocky shores; burrowing worms and wading birds on mudflats).
learnerActions: Look at a continuous coast picture that changes along its length — golden sand, then tumbled rock, then glistening mud.
Point to the line where land meets the sea and say 'this is the coast'.
Name each stretch as sandy, rocky, or muddy by looking at what the ground is made of (not just its colour).
Tap or lift a flap on each shore to hear what makes it special: rock has cracks and water-filled pools to shelter in; sand can be burrowed into; mud is soft and full of hidden food.

Find the hidden residents: a crab wedged in a rock crevice next to seaweed, a razor shell buried in sand below the dune grass, a long-beaked bird probing the mud beside saltmarsh plants, and say each plant's or animal's name with one fact.
Say out loud why that animal is in that spot — 'the crab hides in the rock', 'the bird digs in the soft mud for worms'.
activities.intendedInsight: A coast is the line where land meets the ocean, the SAME coast can be sandy, rocky, or muddy, and each animal lives where that shore lets it hide, burrow, or feed.

activities.title: Sort the animals onto the right shore
feedback: For a correct match, restate the reason so the habitat link sticks: 'Right — the razor shell can bury itself in loose sand.'
For a mismatch, point to the need: 'This crab likes rock cracks to hide in. Can you see any cracks on the open sand? Where would it find them?'
If the learner matches by guessing, prompt the reasoning: 'Tell me what this shore is made of, then what this animal needs.'
activities.rationale: Sorting with a stated reason turns naming into active habitat reasoning and gives immediate, specific feedback. A sort can teach and check classification, but does not by itself elicit an independent spoken definition, so it is paired with the explanation activity. It reinforces the land-and-life connection that the KS1 habitats standard asks for. Can be done with physical cards and trays or on screen.
sourceClaims: UK KS1 Y2 science requires pupils to identify that most living things live in habitats to which they are suited, and to identify and name a variety of plants and animals in their habitats including micro-habitats.

Rocky, sandy and muddy shores are distinct intertidal habitats supporting different communities of plants and animals (e.g. limpets and crabs on rocky shores; burrowing worms and wading birds on mudflats).
learnerActions: Look at three shore trays labelled sandy, rocky, and muddy.

Place (drag or physically move picture cards of) a crab, limpet, sanderling, razor shell, curlew (a long-beaked wading bird), and lugworm onto the shore where each is most often found. Some, like crabs and lugworms, can live on more than one kind of shore.
Before placing each one, say why: 'The crab goes on the rocks because it can hide', 'the curlew goes on the mud because it can probe for worms'.
Check each placement against a short 'why it fits' explanation.
activities.intendedInsight: Different shore materials suit different animals; matching an animal to a shore means thinking about what the animal needs (a place to hide, soft ground to dig, food to find).

activities.title: Say what a coast really is
feedback: If the learner says a coast is always sandy, show a rocky shore and a muddy estuary beside a sandy beach: all three are coasts; define coast by land-meets-sea, then re-sort the types.
If they describe a coast as a holiday resort, trace the whole coastline on a map — most of it has no holiday-makers; it is a boundary, not a destination.
If they say every coast has the same animals, pair each type with a typical resident (rocky → limpet/crab; sandy → burrowing worm/cockle; muddy → wading bird) and ask them to match again.
activities.rationale: A short spoken or written check of the three evidence goals (define coast, name ≥2 types, name an animal per type) surfaces the common 'coast = sandy beach' and 'coast = holiday spot' misconceptions. Asking the learner to name animals in each habitat directly reflects the KS1 requirement to name animals in their habitats. The non-sandy counterexample (cliff) and the map-tracing move separate the general concept from a single familiar example; recognition or sorting alone does not elicit this independent description.
sourceClaims: UK KS1 Y2 science requires pupils to identify that most living things live in habitats to which they are suited, and to identify and name a variety of plants and animals in their habitats including micro-habitats.
learnerActions: Answer in your own words: 'What is a coast?' — aiming for 'where land meets the ocean', not 'a sandy beach'.
Name at least two kinds of coast (sandy, rocky, muddy).
Name one animal you would expect at each kind of coast you named.
Decide whether a rocky cliff with waves at its base is a coast, and explain why.
Trace the edge where land meets the sea on a map all the way round and say whether the whole line is coast, even the parts with no people.
activities.intendedInsight: A coast is defined by the land–sea boundary (including cliffs and mudflats), not by sand or by being a holiday spot, and its type shapes which animals live there.

activities.title: Tell the ranger about your beach day
feedback: Affirm and extend a memory: 'You found a shell on the sand — lots of shelled animals bury into soft sand like that.'
Gently redirect a vague answer toward the shore material and its life: 'Was it rocky or muddy where you saw the crab? What do crabs like about the rocks?'
activities.rationale: Drawing on children's own beach experiences grounds vocabulary in memory and offers a warm supplement to the visual work. This is proposed as a supportive alternative; dialogue may prompt recall and self-report but on its own may not reliably establish accurate naming and matching at this age, so it supplements rather than replaces the visual naming and sorting activities.
learnerActions: Talk with a 'beach ranger' (an adult, puppet, or role-play voice) about what you have found or might find at the beach.
Describe something you saw and say which shore it came from — sand, rock, or mud.
Answer the ranger's follow-ups: 'What was the ground like there?' and 'What animal did you see, and why was it there?'
activities.intendedInsight: New coast vocabulary connects to the learner's own remembered experiences, and even a familiar beach trip can be sorted into shore types with their typical life.

constraints: Keep the topic observational and photographic for ages 5–7; do not introduce tide or erosion mechanisms — these belong to the older (7–9) follow-on.
Use real photographs so sandy/rocky/muddy are distinguished by what each shore is made of, not by colour alone.
Anchor the place (land meets the ocean) before naming the three categories.
Introduce 'suited to its habitat' lightly as a bridge ('why do crabs like the rocks?'), without demanding full mechanism.

A sort-and-match or multiple-choice check verifies recognition and matching; it does not by itself show the learner can describe a coast in their own words, so include at least one spoken or written explanation.

The conversation/ranger activity is a supportive supplement for grounding vocabulary in experience; on its own it may not reliably establish accurate naming and matching for this age, so pair it with the visual activities.
Use coasts distinct from river banks and lake edges, and distinguish the coastline from the open ocean, since learners commonly confuse these.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Both listed sources are marked verified:false in the source row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original rated a 3D/spatial artefact 'poor' with the claim that '3D adds nothing' and rated a static interactive image 'ideal'; these are catalog fit preferences, not established pedagogical laws, so they are reframed as design choices rather than universal claims. Different media offer different experiences for this naming/matching goal, and the image's suitability is a proposal, not proven superiority.

The original framed a quiz/categorization as cleanly checking 'all three evidence goals'; recognition and sorting are retained but a spoken/written self-explanation step was added because recognition-only responses do not by themselves elicit independent description of what a coast is.

Signature animal-to-shore pairings (crab/limpet/anemone on rock; sanderling/razor shell/cockle on sand; wading bird/lugworm on mud) are preserved as typical, plausible examples. Mudskipper was mentioned once in the original pedagogy operational details (not in the cited source claims) and is not UK-typical, so it is omitted from learner-facing examples; general wading-bird/lugworm examples are preferred and mudskipper is not asserted as a standard UK mudflat resident.

Activity 3 retains the KS1 claim because the activity directly asks learners to name animals in each habitat (a KS1 requirement); the claim supports that naming sub-goal only — it does not evidence the assessment-design rationale or the 'define coast' goal, and no source directly supports that these specific activities have been tested.

probeDeeper: 'You said a coast is where land meets the sea. Is a rocky cliff with waves at the bottom a coast? Why?' (non-sandy counterexample)
'Would you find the same animals on a rocky shore as on a muddy one? Why might they differ?'
'Name an animal you'd expect on a rocky coast, and one on a sandy beach.'
'Is a coast a place people go, or something more than that? Explain.'
assess.correctAnswer: It's not quite right — a coast is anywhere the LAND MEETS the ocean, not only a sandy beach. Coasts come in different kinds: sandy, rocky, or muddy. Each kind has different plants and animals — for example crabs and limpets on a rocky coast, or wading birds probing a muddy shore.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks every coast is a sandy beach ('coast = the sandy beach I go to')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show photos of a rocky shore and a muddy estuary alongside a sandy beach — all are coasts. Define coast by land-meets-sea, then sort the three types.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — a coast is always a sandy beach
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denies rocky or muddy coasts; can only picture sand

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks a coast is only a place people visit on holiday, not the general boundary where land meets the sea
errorPatterns.nextMove: Trace the edge of land on a map all the way round — the whole line is coast, most of it with no holiday-makers at all. It's a boundary, not a destination.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes 'coast' as a seaside resort; can't state the land-meets-ocean idea

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks the same animals live on every coast, whatever its type
errorPatterns.nextMove: Pair each coast type with a typical animal (rocky → limpet/crab; sandy → burrowing worm/cockle; muddy → wading bird). Habitat type shapes which animals live there.
errorPatterns.distractor: Every coast has the same animals on it
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Second tier: can't match different creatures to sandy vs rocky vs muddy shores

responseLevels.gap: Insists a coast is always a sandy beach, or only a holiday spot; no land-meets-sea idea.
responseLevels.full: Defines a coast as the land–ocean boundary, names sandy/rocky/muddy types, AND matches at least one animal to a coast type — linking the kind of shore to the life it supports, and recognising a non-sandy shore as still a coast.
responseLevels.partial: Defines a coast as where land meets the sea and knows beaches vary, but lists the types as separate facts — can't connect coast type to the different plants and animals found there.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A child says: 'A coast is always a sandy beach — that's what a coast IS.' Is that right? Tell me what a coast really is, and whether every coast looks the same.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands 'coast' defines it as the land–sea boundary and knows it isn't always sandy. A child whose only model is a holiday beach insists every coast is sandy. The second tier ('does every coast look the same?') separates the general concept from the single familiar example, and asking for animals-per-type checks whether they link habitat type to the life it holds.
